In this assignment, you'll be picking up where you left off with the M&Ms activity. You'll load the data and perform some basic statistical analysis. Follow the steps below to complete the assignment.

### Task 1: Load the tidyverse
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

### Task 2: Load the M&Ms dataset from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/mandms.csv

```{r}
m_and_ms <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/mandms.csv")
```

### Task 3: Sample 5 rows of data from the dataset

```{r}
set.seed(42)
sample_5 <- m_and_ms |>
  sample_n(5)
```

### Task 4: Calculate the mean age and standard deviation of the sample, using either the red or black number of M&Ms

```{r}
mean(sample_5$red)
sd(sample_5$red)
```

### Task 5: Calculate the mean age and standard deviation of the population, using the same measure as in Task 4

```{r}
mean(m_and_ms$red)
sd(m_and_ms$red)
```


### Task 6: Compare the sample and population statistics

The sample mean is 79.6 red M&Ms and the population mean is 72.98. These values are slightly different, but not too far off from each other. The same goes for the standard deviations. The sample standard deviation is 10.06 red M&Ms, while the population standard deviation is 16.46.

### Task 7: Describe the results

Write a few sentences about what you found in the data. What does this tell you about the M&Ms dataset and about the act of random sampling?

The average number of red M&Ms found in a handful from the entire population is about 73. When you take just 5 samples, the average number of red M&Ms goes up to almost 80 red M&Ms. This tells me that the act of random sampling will get you within a reasonable ballpark of the actual population mean, but it still will not be completely accurate. I'm sure if we took more than 5 samples, the sample mean and standard deviation would become closer to the population values. Looking at standard deviations, because the population SD is larger than the sample SD, this tells me that the population data is more spread out than the sample data, which makes sense because there are far fewer numbers in the sample.
